decisions.quote: We confirmed the well-known association with DTC of the 9q22.31 region that includes the FOXE1 gene ( 9–12 ). In this independent and separate case–control study conducted in Germany, we replicated associations with PTC risk that we reported previously in SERPINA5 ( 21 ) and FTO ( 17 ) genes. Other candidate variants in EVPL , TICAM1 and SCARB1 previously identified ( 17 , 21 ) were also associated with PTC risk. We found several new associations between SNPs in SERPINA5 , FTO , TICAM1 and HSPA6 genes, and risk of FTC. In contrast to several studies, we did not observe associations for NKX2-1 SNPs ( 9 , 25 , 26 ).
decisions.reason: Omitted target: SNPs in FOXE1 and NKX2-1 were selected for validation from reference 9, with FOXE1 confirmed and NKX2-1 not observed (mixed).

decisions.reason: The current study selected the top 50 PTC-associated tag SNPs from the NCI rare cancer i-Select series (references 16–21) for independent validation in a German case–control study. Direct cross-referencing of the newly recovered current Supplemental Table 2 against the primary text and Table 2 of Aschebrook-Kilfoy et al. (2012; reference 20, 'Common genetic variants in metabolism and detoxification pathways and the risk of papillary thyroid cancer', Endocr. Relat. Cancer 19:333–344) establishes that three exact highlighted PTC-associated SNPs (Ptrend <= 0.01) reported by Aschebrook-Kilfoy et al. (2012) were empirically re-tested for PTC association in Supplemental Table 2: CYP8B1 rs11715464 (entry #16, rows R64–R67, PTC Ptrend = 0.8974 vs. original Ptrend = 0.0029), CYP8B1 rs6788947 (entry #17, rows R68–R71, PTC Ptrend = 0.624 vs. original Ptrend = 0.0033), and UGT2B7 rs3924194 (entry #21, rows R84–R87, PTC Ptrend = 0.07221 vs. original Ptrend = 0.0027), plus two additional CYP8B1 tag SNPs (rs3732860, rs7641812). This metabolism/detoxification paper is a distinct original study and finding from shipped row 84 (Neta et al. 2011, 10.1093/carcin/bgr100, reference 16).

decisions.quote: Boards of the respective hospitals/clinics. At the time of blood draw, basic demographic data were collected on the cases and controls, including date of birth, gender, ethnicity, height, weight and personal history of cancer. For cases, information on previous history of any radiation treatment and family history of cancer was additionally collected, whereas information on tumor, nodes and metastasis staging was available from medical records. Personal history of other thyroid conditions, such as Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, was not collected systematically. For 45 cases and 5 controls, a history of prior cancer diagnosis was reported. decisions.reason: The current paper collectively cites the NCI i-Select papillary thyroid cancer (PTC) series (references 16–21) as the source from which the top 50 tag SNPs (out of 17,525 SNPs across 1,129 candidate genes) were selected for validation alongside 45 candidate-region SNPs and 5 literature SNPs (100 SNPs total), of which 21 SNPs failed assay design, genotyping, Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, or call-rate thresholds and 79 were analyzed in Supplemental Table 2. Comparing the 79 analyzed SNPs in current Supplemental Table 2 against the primary text of Schonfeld et al. (2012; reference 19) shows zero overlap with any of Schonfeld et al.'s 10 highlighted PTC-associated SNPs (Ptrend < 0.01 in all subjects or women: rs4646, rs10046, rs9939609, rs1271572, rs8023545, rs2254403, rs3775777, rs1395, rs17667932, rs4815552) or any of its 5 sex-hormone pathway genes (CYP19A1, ESR1, HSD17B3, SULF1, GNRH2; FTO was analyzed separately in the obesity paper, reference 17). Because the 21 excluded SNPs are not itemized by gene or reference, the primary evidence cannot establish whether any specific finding from Schonfeld et al. (2012) was selected for replication.
